question: A student asks which cellular signaling change is produced by short-acting inhaled bronchodilators that relax airway smooth muscle. Which of the following best describes that mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Stimulation of Gs leading to increased cAMP
options.rationale: Correct: β2 agonists activate Gs → adenylyl cyclase → ↑cAMP → PKA-mediated MLCK inhibition causing bronchodilation as described in the lecture.

options.text: Blockade of M3 receptors reducing intracellular calcium
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticholinergics block M3 to reduce bronchoconstriction via decreased Ca²⁺ signaling; this would be correct only if the drug class were antimuscarinic rather than β2 agonist.

options.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase increasing cAMP levels
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibitors raise cAMP by preventing degradation (methylxanthines); this is not the primary mechanism of short-acting β2 agonists.

options.text: Antagonism of IgE preventing mast cell activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Anti-IgE antibodies (omalizumab) bind circulating IgE to reduce allergic activation; this does not explain acute bronchodilation by β2 agonists.

options.text: Stabilization of mast cells preventing mediator release
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells to prevent mediator release; it does not produce rapid smooth muscle relaxation via Gs/cAMP signaling.

question: Which inhaled agent class is described as blocking muscarinic receptors on airway smooth muscle to reduce bronchoconstriction and mucus secretion?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Anticholinergic agents that antagonize M3 receptors
options.rationale: Correct: Anticholinergics (e.g., ipratropium, tiotropium) block M3 receptors causing bronchorelaxation and decreased mucus secretion as stated in the lecture.

options.text: Beta2 agonists that stimulate Gs and increase cAMP
options.rationale: Wrong: β2 agonists act via Gs and cAMP to relax smooth muscle; they do not block muscarinic receptors or directly reduce cholinergic-mediated mucus secretion.

options.text: Corticosteroids that alter gene transcription broadly
options.rationale: Wrong: Corticosteroids reduce inflammation via transcriptional effects; they are not muscarinic antagonists and do not directly block M3 receptors.

options.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists blocking CysLT1 receptors
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast and zafirlukast block CysLT1 to reduce leukotriene effects; they do not antagonize muscarinic receptors.

options.text: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors preventing cAMP breakdown
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibitors (theophylline) increase cAMP by inhibiting degradation; they are not antimuscarinic agents blocking M3 receptors.

question: According to the lecture, which inhaled anti-inflammatory agent increases transcription of anti-inflammatory proteins and upregulates β2 receptors?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids increasing anti-inflammatory gene transcription
options.rationale: Correct: Inhaled corticosteroids upregulate transcription of anti-inflammatory proteins and β2-adrenergic receptors, reducing airway inflammation as the slides state.

options.text: Leukotriene modifiers blocking CysLT1 receptor signaling
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene modifiers inhibit CysLT1 and reduce leukotriene-mediated effects but do not upregulate β2 receptors or broadly increase anti-inflammatory gene transcription.

options.text: Mast cell stabilizers preventing chloride dependent degranulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and affects chloride gating to prevent degranulation; it does not increase anti-inflammatory gene transcription or β2 receptor expression.

options.text: Monoclonal anti-IgE antibodies binding circulating IgE molecules
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab binds IgE to reduce allergic activation; it does not directly alter gene transcription to increase β2 receptor expression.

options.text: Phosphodiesterase inhibitors increasing intracellular cAMP levels
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibitors raise cAMP and have immunomodulatory effects but do not primarily act by increasing anti-inflammatory gene transcription or β2 receptor numbers.

question: Which adverse effect is most characteristic of systemic methylxanthine toxicity as described in the lecture?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Seizures and cardiac arrhythmias at supratherapeutic levels
options.rationale: Correct: Theophylline toxicity can cause seizures and life-threatening arrhythmias at supratherapeutic doses per the lecture.

options.text: Oropharyngeal candidiasis with inhaled deposition
options.rationale: Wrong: Thrush is an adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids, not methylxanthines; this would be correct only for inhaled steroid exposure.

options.text: Anaphylaxis after subcutaneous administration
options.rationale: Wrong: Anaphylaxis is a rare adverse effect of monoclonal antibodies like omalizumab; it is not typical of methylxanthines.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma after nebulized administration
options.rationale: Wrong: Nebulized anticholinergics can cause mydriasis and precipitate angle closure glaucoma; this is not a methylxanthine toxicity feature.

options.text: Hepatotoxicity with chronic oral dosing
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is associated with zileuton (5-lipoxygenase inhibitor); methylxanthines are not primarily hepatotoxic.

question: A patient with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease would most likely benefit from which oral agent class that blocks cysteinyl leukotriene receptor signaling?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists such as montelukast
options.rationale: Correct: Montelukast and zafirlukast inhibit CysLT1 receptors and are indicated for aspirin-sensitive asthma per the lecture.

options.text: 5-lipoxygenase inhibitors such as zileuton oral tablets
options.rationale: Wrong: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase and affects leukotriene synthesis; while related, the lecture highlights CysLT1 antagonists specifically for aspirin-exacerbated disease as common therapy.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids delivered via metered dose inhaler
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled steroids reduce inflammation broadly but leukotriene pathway modifiers are specifically useful in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease; steroids alone would not target leukotriene-mediated sensitivity.

options.text: Short acting beta agonists used before exercise
options.rationale: Wrong: SABAs relieve bronchospasm acutely and prophylactically for exercise but do not address aspirin-triggered leukotriene overproduction.

options.text: Mast cell stabilizers taken four times daily prophylactically
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and can be used prophylactically but is not the preferred therapy for aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease which involves leukotriene pathways.

question: Which drug class must be combined with long-acting bronchodilators to avoid worsening outcomes in asthma because they do not treat airway inflammation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Long acting beta agonists that lack anti-inflammatory effects
options.rationale: Correct: LABAs (salmeterol, formoterol) do not treat underlying inflammation and must be used with inhaled corticosteroids to prevent fatal exacerbations as emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids used as monotherapy for control
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled corticosteroids address inflammation and are appropriate controller therapy; they are not the class that must be combined to avoid harm.

options.text: Anticholinergics that antagonize M3 receptors chronically
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticholinergics provide bronchodilation and can be used in COPD; they are not the LABA class described as requiring concurrent steroids to avoid worsening asthma.

options.text: Methylxanthines that inhibit phosphodiesterase enzymes systemically
options.rationale: Wrong: Methylxanthines have bronchodilator and some anti-inflammatory effects; they are not the LABA class that must be paired with ICS to prevent adverse outcomes.

options.text: Leukotriene modifiers taken orally for chronic control
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene modifiers target leukotriene pathways and can be adjuncts or alternatives; they are not the LABA class requiring ICS coadministration per the lecture warning.

question: A patient using high-dose oral epinephrine for bronchospasm would most likely experience which adverse effect due to nonselective adrenergic stimulation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Tachycardia and arrhythmias from β1 cardiac stimulation
options.rationale: Correct: Nonselective adrenergic agonists like epinephrine stimulate β1 causing cardiac stimulation, tachycardia, and arrhythmias as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Oropharyngeal candidiasis from inhaled deposition
options.rationale: Wrong: Thrush is associated with inhaled corticosteroids, not systemic nonselective adrenergic agonists like epinephrine.

options.text: Seizures and toxic encephalopathy from theophylline overdose
options.rationale: Wrong: Seizures are a feature of methylxanthine toxicity; they are not the primary adverse effect of nonselective adrenergic agonists.

options.text: Hepatotoxicity and transaminase elevation with chronic use
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is a concern with zileuton; it is not characteristic of systemic adrenergic agonists like epinephrine.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma precipitated by nebulized therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Nebulized anticholinergics can precipitate angle closure glaucoma; this is unrelated to systemic adrenergic stimulation from epinephrine.

question: Which inhaled bronchodilator has a rapid onset suitable for rescue and is available as a pure R-enantiomer formulation to increase β2 selectivity?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Levalbuterol as the R-enantiomer of albuterol
options.rationale: Correct: Levalbuterol is the pure R-enantiomer of albuterol with greater β2 selectivity and is used for acute relief as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Salmeterol with a lipophilic side chain and slow onset
options.rationale: Wrong: Salmeterol is a LABA with slower onset due to lipophilic side chain; it is not the rapid-onset R-enantiomer rescue agent.

options.text: Formoterol with rapid onset but long duration
options.rationale: Wrong: Formoterol has rapid onset among LABAs but is not an R-enantiomer formulation of albuterol; levalbuterol is the specific enantiomeric rescue drug.

options.text: Ipratropium bromide as a short acting antimuscarinic inhaler
options.rationale: Wrong: Ipratropium is a SAMA anticholinergic used for bronchodilation but is not an enantiomeric β2 agonist.

options.text: Theophylline as an oral phosphodiesterase inhibitor
options.rationale: Wrong: Theophylline is a methylxanthine PDE inhibitor taken orally; it is not an inhaled R-enantiomer β2 agonist for rescue.

question: A clinician wants to reduce systemic adverse effects of inhaled steroids by using a prodrug activated in airway epithelium. Which agent from the lecture fits this description?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Ciclesonide as an airway activated ester prodrug
options.rationale: Correct: Ciclesonide is an ester prodrug activated in airway epithelium to reduce systemic adverse effects as described in the lecture.

options.text: Fluticasone as a potent inhaled corticosteroid with deposition
options.rationale: Wrong: Fluticasone is a potent inhaled steroid but is not described as an airway-activated ester prodrug like ciclesonide.

options.text: Budesonide as an inhaled steroid with systemic effects
options.rationale: Wrong: Budesonide is an inhaled corticosteroid but the lecture specifically highlights ciclesonide for reduced systemic exposure via prodrug activation.

options.text: Prednisone as an oral systemic corticosteroid for severe disease
options.rationale: Wrong: Prednisone is systemic and associated with greater systemic side effects; it is not an inhaled airway-activated prodrug.

options.text: Beclomethasone as an inhaled steroid used in combination therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Beclomethasone is an inhaled steroid but is not the prodrug activated in airway epithelium described in the lecture.

question: A patient with eosinophilic asthma is considered for biologic therapy that targets IL-5 signaling. Which monoclonal antibody class from the lecture would be appropriate?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Anti-IL-5 agents such as mepolizumab or benralizumab
options.rationale: Correct: Mepolizumab and benralizumab inhibit IL-5 or its receptor to reduce eosinophilic asthma as listed in the lecture.

options.text: Anti-IgE therapy such as omalizumab for allergic asthma
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab targets IgE and is used for allergic asthma; IL-5 targeted agents are preferred for eosinophilic phenotypes.

options.text: Dupilumab inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling pathways
options.rationale: Wrong: Dupilumab blocks IL-4/IL-13 signaling and is used for certain eosinophilic asthma but the lecture specifically pairs mepolizumab/benralizumab with IL-5 targeting.

options.text: Cromolyn as a mast cell stabilizer for prophylaxis
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and is used prophylactically; it does not target IL-5 signaling for eosinophil reduction.

options.text: Montelukast as an oral leukotriene receptor antagonist
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast blocks CysLT1 receptors and helps leukotriene-mediated disease; it does not directly inhibit IL-5 signaling.

question: A patient with COPD who smokes wants pharmacologic help to quit. Which agent described in the lecture acts as a partial agonist at nicotinic receptors to reduce cravings?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Varenicline as a partial alpha4beta2 nicotinic agonist
options.rationale: Correct: Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors reducing cravings and blocking nicotine reward as described in the lecture.

options.text: Bupropion inhibiting norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake
options.rationale: Wrong: Bupropion aids cessation via NE and dopamine reuptake inhibition but is not a nicotinic partial agonist like varenicline.

options.text: Nicotine replacement therapy providing controlled nicotine doses
options.rationale: Wrong: NRT supplies nicotine to reduce withdrawal but does not act as a partial receptor agonist competing with nicotine at α4β2 receptors.

options.text: Theophylline as an oral phosphodiesterase inhibitor bronchodilator
options.rationale: Wrong: Theophylline is a bronchodilator and PDE inhibitor; it is not used primarily for smoking cessation via nicotinic receptor partial agonism.

options.text: Ipratropium bromide as an inhaled antimuscarinic bronchodilator
options.rationale: Wrong: Ipratropium is an anticholinergic bronchodilator and not a smoking cessation agent acting at nicotinic receptors.

question: A researcher measures airway smooth muscle MLCK activity after exposure to a bronchodilator that increases PKA activity. Which change would the lecture predict?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Decreased MLCK activity due to PKA phosphorylation mediated inhibition
options.rationale: Correct: β2 agonist–induced PKA phosphorylates MLCK reducing its activity and lowering MLC phosphorylation, producing bronchodilation as explained in the lecture.

options.text: Increased MLCK activity from enhanced calcium calmodulin binding
options.rationale: Wrong: Increased MLCK activity would occur with higher Ca²⁺–calmodulin; PKA activation reduces MLCK activity, so this would be correct only if PKA were inhibited.

options.text: Unchanged MLCK activity with increased phospholipase A2 signaling
options.rationale: Wrong: Phospholipase A2 relates to eicosanoid synthesis; it does not explain PKA-mediated MLCK inhibition. MLCK would not remain unchanged under PKA activation.

options.text: Decreased MLCK activity due to direct adenosine receptor antagonism
options.rationale: Wrong: Adenosine receptor antagonism (methylxanthines) has different downstream effects; the lecture attributes MLCK inhibition specifically to PKA phosphorylation from β2 agonists.

options.text: Increased MLCK activity from muscarinic M3 receptor blockade
options.rationale: Wrong: M3 blockade reduces Ca²⁺ signaling and would decrease MLCK activity; increased MLCK activity would be inconsistent with M3 antagonism.

question: A patient with nocturnal asthma remains symptomatic despite daytime short-acting bronchodilator use. Based on lecture pharmacology, which property makes a long-acting agent less suitable for immediate nocturnal relief?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Slower onset of action delaying relief during acute nocturnal symptoms
options.rationale: Correct: LABAs like salmeterol have slower onset and are less suitable for immediate nocturnal relief; the lecture contrasts rapid-onset formoterol with slower salmeterol.

options.text: Longer duration causing tachyphylaxis overnight with repeated dosing
options.rationale: Wrong: Longer duration provides prolonged bronchodilation; tachyphylaxis is not the primary reason LABAs are less suitable for immediate nocturnal rescue.

options.text: Increased systemic absorption producing daytime side effects only
options.rationale: Wrong: Systemic absorption can cause side effects but does not explain lack of immediate nocturnal relief; onset speed is the key factor.

options.text: Requirement for coadministration with leukotriene modifiers nightly
options.rationale: Wrong: LABAs require coadministration with inhaled corticosteroids for safety in asthma, not leukotriene modifiers; this does not explain immediate nocturnal inefficacy.

options.text: Direct antagonism of β2 receptors reducing bronchodilator response
options.rationale: Wrong: LABAs are β2 agonists, not antagonists; direct β2 antagonism would reduce response but is not a property of LABAs.

question: A patient with severe allergic asthma on high-dose inhaled steroids is considered for omalizumab. Which mechanism described in the lecture explains how this biologic reduces exacerbations?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Binding circulating IgE to prevent FcεRI mediated mast cell activation
options.rationale: Correct: Omalizumab binds circulating IgE, preventing IgE from binding FcεRI on mast cells and reducing allergic activation and exacerbations as the lecture states.

options.text: Blocking IL-5 receptor to reduce eosinophil proliferation and survival
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-5 pathway inhibitors (mepolizumab, benralizumab) target eosinophils; omalizumab specifically binds IgE rather than IL-5 or its receptor.

options.text: Inhibiting 5-lipoxygenase to decrease leukotriene synthesis systemically
options.rationale: Wrong: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; this mechanism reduces leukotrienes but is distinct from anti-IgE therapy.

options.text: Antagonizing CysLT1 receptors to block leukotriene mediated bronchoconstriction
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast and zafirlukast antagonize CysLT1; omalizumab works via IgE binding, not leukotriene receptor antagonism.

options.text: Stabilizing mast cell chloride channels to prevent degranulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells via chloride channel effects; omalizumab reduces IgE-mediated activation rather than directly stabilizing mast cells.

question: A patient with exercise-induced bronchospasm is advised on prophylactic therapy. Which agent class from the lecture is specifically noted for prophylactic use before exertion?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Short acting beta agonists taken prior to exercise for prophylaxis
options.rationale: Correct: SABAs like albuterol are effective as prophylaxis before exercise as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids used acutely before exertion for prevention
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled corticosteroids are controllers for chronic inflammation and are not used as immediate pre-exercise prophylaxis.

options.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists taken immediately before exercise
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene modifiers are oral controllers and are not the standard immediate pre-exercise prophylactic agents described in the lecture.

options.text: Cromolyn administered four times daily for acute exercise relief
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn can be used prophylactically for exercise-induced asthma but requires regular dosing and is not the immediate short-acting inhaler recommended before exertion.

options.text: Long acting beta agonists used only for acute pre-exercise prevention
options.rationale: Wrong: LABAs are long-acting and not intended as immediate pre-exercise rescue; SABAs are preferred for prophylaxis.

question: A patient on theophylline is started on ketoconazole. Based on lecture drug interactions, what change in theophylline levels should the clinician expect?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Increased theophylline levels due to CYP3A inhibition by ketoconazole
options.rationale: Correct: Theophylline is metabolized by CYP3A; CYP3A inhibitors like azole antifungals raise theophylline levels increasing toxicity risk as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Decreased theophylline levels due to enzyme induction by ketoconazole
options.rationale: Wrong: Ketoconazole is a CYP inhibitor, not an inducer; enzyme induction would lower levels but is not expected with ketoconazole.

options.text: No change in theophylline levels because of renal excretion dominance
options.rationale: Wrong: Theophylline is primarily metabolized hepatically by CYP enzymes; renal excretion dominance would make CYP interactions irrelevant, which is not the case.

options.text: Increased theophylline clearance via enhanced glucuronidation
options.rationale: Wrong: Ketoconazole does not enhance glucuronidation; it inhibits CYP enzymes, so increased clearance is unlikely.

options.text: Decreased theophylline absorption from gastrointestinal binding
options.rationale: Wrong: Ketoconazole does not bind theophylline in the gut to reduce absorption; the clinically relevant interaction is CYP-mediated metabolism inhibition.

question: A patient with chronic asthma uses an inhaler and develops oral thrush. Which class and administration route from the lecture most likely caused this adverse effect?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids depositing in oropharynx causing candidiasis
options.rationale: Correct: Inhaled corticosteroids can deposit in the oropharynx and cause oropharyngeal candidiasis (thrush) as described in the lecture.

options.text: Inhaled anticholinergics causing dry mouth and fungal overgrowth
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticholinergics cause dry mouth but are not the primary cause of oropharyngeal candidiasis; inhaled steroids are the typical culprit.

options.text: Systemic methylxanthines causing immunosuppression and thrush
options.rationale: Wrong: Methylxanthines do not typically cause immunosuppression leading to thrush; systemic corticosteroids would be more likely to predispose to fungal infections.

options.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists causing mucosal fungal infections
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene modifiers are not associated with oropharyngeal candidiasis; this adverse effect is linked to inhaled corticosteroid deposition.

options.text: Monoclonal anti-IgE injections producing local oral candidiasis
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab can cause immune reactions but is not commonly associated with oropharyngeal candidiasis from inhaler deposition.

question: A patient with severe asthma has elevated eosinophils driven by IL-5. Which therapeutic approach from the lecture directly reduces eosinophil proliferation and activation?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibodies targeting eosinophil signaling
options.rationale: Correct: Mepolizumab and benralizumab inhibit IL-5 signaling or its receptor, reducing eosinophil proliferation and activation as the lecture indicates.

options.text: Anti-IgE therapy reducing mast cell mediated allergic responses
options.rationale: Wrong: Anti-IgE reduces allergic activation but does not directly inhibit IL-5 driven eosinophil proliferation; IL-5 targeted agents are required for that effect.

options.text: Leukotriene receptor antagonists blocking CysLT1 mediated migration
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene antagonists reduce eosinophil migration indirectly but do not directly block IL-5–mediated eosinophil proliferation.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids increasing β2 receptor transcription
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled corticosteroids reduce inflammation and can induce eosinophil apoptosis but the direct reduction of IL-5–driven proliferation is best achieved with anti–IL-5 biologics.

options.text: Cromolyn preventing mast cell degranulation and eosinophil activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and reduces mediator release but does not directly target IL-5 signaling responsible for eosinophil proliferation.

question: A patient with severe asthma is switched from salmeterol monotherapy to a combination inhaler. Based on lecture recommendations, what is the rationale for adding the second agent?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the current evidence-based GDMT for asthma/COPD (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Add inhaled corticosteroid to treat underlying airway inflammation
options.rationale: Correct: LABAs do not treat inflammation and must be combined with inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) to address the inflammatory cause and reduce risk of fatal exacerbations as the lecture warns.

options.text: Add leukotriene antagonist to directly antagonize β2 receptor effects
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene antagonists do not antagonize β2 receptors; they target leukotriene pathways and would not substitute for anti-inflammatory effects of ICS required with LABA therapy.

options.text: Add anticholinergic to increase β2 receptor density on smooth muscle
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticholinergics block M3 receptors and do not increase β2 receptor density; the lecture specifies adding ICS to LABA to treat inflammation.

options.text: Add methylxanthine to inhibit adenylyl cyclase and reduce cAMP
options.rationale: Wrong: Methylxanthines inhibit PDE to increase cAMP, not inhibit adenylyl cyclase; they are not the recommended agent to pair with LABA to treat inflammation.

options.text: Add omalizumab to block muscarinic receptor mediated bronchoconstriction
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab binds IgE and reduces allergic activation; it does not block muscarinic receptors and is not the standard addition to LABA for general asthma control.

question: A patient with severe COPD has persistent bronchospasm despite β2 agonists and is intolerant of tachycardia. Which inhaled class from the lecture is a reasonable alternative due to minimal systemic absorption?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Ipratropium bromide as a quaternary antimuscarinic with low absorption
options.rationale: Correct: Ipratropium is a quaternary ammonium anticholinergic with limited systemic absorption and fewer cardiac β1 effects, making it suitable when β2 agonists cause tachycardia.

options.text: Oral theophylline with systemic PDE inhibition and cardiac effects
options.rationale: Wrong: Theophylline is systemic and can cause tachycardia and arrhythmias; it is not preferable when tachycardia is a concern.

options.text: Inhaled salmeterol as a long acting β2 agonist with slow onset
options.rationale: Wrong: Salmeterol is a LABA that can still have systemic β effects; its slow onset also makes it less suitable for acute intolerance to tachycardia from SABAs.

options.text: Subcutaneous omalizumab to reduce IgE mediated bronchospasm
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab targets IgE-mediated allergic pathways and is not an inhaled bronchodilator alternative for acute bronchospasm in COPD.

options.text: Oral montelukast blocking leukotriene receptors for immediate relief
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast is oral and used for leukotriene-mediated disease; it does not provide rapid bronchodilation and is not preferred for acute bronchospasm in COPD.

question: A patient on zileuton develops elevated liver enzymes. Based on the lecture, which mechanism explains this adverse effect and what pathway does the drug inhibit?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase and can cause hepatotoxicity
options.rationale: Correct: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase reducing leukotriene synthesis; the lecture notes hepatotoxicity as a limiting adverse effect of zileuton.

options.text: Zileuton blocks CysLT1 receptors and causes immune mediated hepatitis
options.rationale: Wrong: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase rather than blocking CysLT1; immune-mediated hepatitis is not the specific mechanism described for zileuton hepatotoxicity.

options.text: Montelukast antagonizes leukotriene receptors causing direct hepatocyte necrosis
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast is a CysLT1 antagonist and is mainly associated with neuropsychiatric effects; direct hepatocyte necrosis is not the lecture-described mechanism for zileuton.

options.text: Corticosteroids induce hepatic enzymes leading to transaminase elevation
options.rationale: Wrong: Systemic corticosteroids have many systemic effects but the lecture specifically links hepatotoxicity to zileuton via 5-lipoxygenase inhibition.

options.text: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells causing cholestatic liver injury
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and has low systemic absorption; it is not associated with cholestatic liver injury as described for zileuton.

question: A patient with severe asthma has frequent exacerbations despite inhaled steroids and LABA. The team considers adding a biologic that inhibits IL-4 and IL-13. Which agent from the lecture fits this mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Dupilumab inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling in eosinophilic asthma
options.rationale: Correct: Dupilumab blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signaling and is indicated for certain eosinophilic asthma phenotypes as listed in the lecture.

options.text: Omalizumab binding circulating IgE to reduce allergic exacerbations
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab targets IgE rather than IL-4/IL-13; it is used for allergic asthma but does not directly inhibit IL-4/IL-13 signaling.

options.text: Mepolizumab targeting IL-5 to reduce eosinophil counts
options.rationale: Wrong: Mepolizumab targets IL-5; while useful for eosinophilic asthma, it does not inhibit IL-4/IL-13 signaling specifically.

options.text: Benralizumab blocking IgE receptors on mast cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Benralizumab targets IL-5 receptor on eosinophils; it does not block IgE receptors and is not an IL-4/IL-13 inhibitor.

options.text: Montelukast antagonizing leukotriene receptors to reduce inflammation
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast blocks CysLT1 receptors; it does not inhibit IL-4 or IL-13 signaling and is less targeted for severe eosinophilic phenotypes described here.

question: A patient with asthma uses high-dose inhaled β2 agonists and reports tremor. Based on lecture pharmacology, what explains this adverse effect?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: β2 receptor stimulation in skeletal muscle causing tremor
options.rationale: Correct: β2 receptors are expressed in peripheral skeletal muscle and high-dose β2 agonists can cause tremor as noted in the lecture.

options.text: M3 receptor blockade causing neuromuscular hyperexcitability
options.rationale: Wrong: M3 blockade causes anticholinergic effects like dry mouth, not skeletal muscle tremor; tremor is linked to β2 stimulation.

options.text: PDE inhibition causing central nervous system mediated tremor
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibitors can cause CNS stimulation but the lecture attributes tremor specifically to peripheral β2 receptor activation in skeletal muscle.

options.text: IgE mediated mast cell activation producing muscle fasciculations
options.rationale: Wrong: IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation causes allergic symptoms, not the skeletal muscle tremor associated with β2 agonists.

options.text: Corticosteroid induced myopathy presenting as tremor
options.rationale: Wrong: Corticosteroid myopathy causes weakness rather than tremor; tremor from inhaled β2 agonists is due to peripheral β2 receptor stimulation.

question: A patient with severe asthma is started on omalizumab and experiences an immediate severe hypersensitivity reaction after the first injection. According to the lecture, what is the most appropriate concern and mechanism?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Anaphylaxis due to immune response to the monoclonal antibody
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes that omalizumab can rarely cause immune responses including anaphylaxis after subcutaneous administration.

options.text: Hepatotoxicity from 5-lipoxygenase inhibition causing liver failure
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is associated with zileuton (5-LO inhibitor), not omalizumab; anaphylaxis is the immediate immune concern with omalizumab.

options.text: Seizure from methylxanthine interaction with monoclonal therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Seizures are linked to theophylline toxicity; there is no lecture-described direct seizure risk from omalizumab.

options.text: Bronchospasm from leukotriene receptor blockade paradoxically worsening
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene receptor antagonists do not typically cause immediate anaphylaxis; this distractor conflates unrelated mechanisms.

options.text: Angle closure glaucoma from systemic anticholinergic absorption
options.rationale: Wrong: Angle closure glaucoma is a risk with nebulized anticholinergics causing mydriasis; it is unrelated to omalizumab injections.

question: A patient with asthma is prescribed montelukast but has a history of depression. Based on the lecture, what counseling point is most relevant?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Montelukast may increase risk of neuropsychiatric symptoms including suicide
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture warns montelukast should be avoided in patients with a history of depression due to risk of suicide and neuropsychiatric effects.

options.text: Montelukast commonly causes hepatotoxicity requiring monthly monitoring
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is primarily associated with zileuton; montelukast's main neuropsychiatric concern is emphasized in the lecture.

options.text: Montelukast causes oropharyngeal candidiasis with inhaler use
options.rationale: Wrong: Thrush is linked to inhaled corticosteroids; montelukast is an oral tablet and not associated with inhaler-related candidiasis.

options.text: Montelukast increases seizure risk similar to theophylline toxicity
options.rationale: Wrong: Seizures are a feature of methylxanthine toxicity; montelukast's notable adverse effect in the lecture is neuropsychiatric, not seizure risk.

options.text: Montelukast causes tachycardia due to β1 adrenergic stimulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Tachycardia from β1 stimulation is associated with nonselective adrenergic agonists; montelukast does not act on adrenergic receptors.

question: A patient with severe asthma has elevated IgE and frequent exacerbations despite inhaled steroids. The team considers omalizumab. Which outcome described in the lecture is expected after adding this therapy?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major therapeutic uses of the drugs in each class (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Reduced corticosteroid dose and fewer exacerbations over time
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture states omalizumab lowers corticosteroid requirements and reduces exacerbation frequency in moderate asthma.

options.text: Immediate bronchodilation via β2 receptor activation within minutes
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab works by binding IgE and reducing allergic inflammation over weeks; it does not produce immediate β2-mediated bronchodilation.

options.text: Rapid decrease in leukotriene synthesis within hours of injection
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab does not directly inhibit leukotriene synthesis; zileuton affects leukotriene production, not anti-IgE therapy.

options.text: Permanent elimination of eosinophils via IL-5 receptor blockade
options.rationale: Wrong: IL-5 pathway inhibitors target eosinophils; omalizumab reduces IgE-mediated activation but does not permanently eliminate eosinophils via IL-5 receptor blockade.

options.text: Increased risk of hepatotoxicity requiring liver enzyme monitoring
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is associated with zileuton; omalizumab's notable risk is rare anaphylaxis rather than hepatotoxicity.

question: A patient with asthma uses a nebulized anticholinergic and develops acute unilateral eye pain and blurred vision. Based on the lecture, what is the most likely mechanism for this ocular event?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Mydriasis from local antimuscarinic effect precipitating angle closure glaucoma
options.rationale: Correct: Nebulized anticholinergics can cause mydriasis and increased intraocular pressure precipitating angle closure glaucoma as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Direct ocular infection from inhaled corticosteroid fungal deposition
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled corticosteroids can cause oropharyngeal candidiasis but not acute unilateral angle closure glaucoma from mydriasis due to antimuscarinic exposure.

options.text: Ischemic optic neuropathy from systemic β1 adrenergic stimulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Systemic β1 stimulation causes cardiac effects; ischemic optic neuropathy is not the acute ocular event described for nebulized anticholinergics.

options.text: Allergic conjunctivitis from IgE mediated reaction to nebulized drug
options.rationale: Wrong: Allergic conjunctivitis would present with itching and bilateral symptoms; the lecture specifically links nebulized anticholinergics to mydriasis and angle closure risk.

options.text: Retinal detachment from sudden changes in intraocular pressure after inhalation
options.rationale: Wrong: Retinal detachment is not the acute mechanism described; the lecture emphasizes angle closure glaucoma due to antimuscarinic-induced mydriasis.

question: A patient with asthma is prescribed cromolyn for exercise-induced symptoms. According to the lecture, what is the primary cellular action of this agent?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Stabilization of mast cells preventing mediator release and degranulation
options.rationale: Correct: Cromolyn stabilizes mast cells by inhibiting chloride transport and reducing Ca²⁺ gating to prevent mediator release as described in the lecture.

options.text: Direct antagonism of β2 receptors reducing bronchial hyperreactivity
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn does not antagonize β2 receptors; it stabilizes mast cells to prevent mediator release rather than directly affecting β2 signaling.

options.text: Inhibition of 5-lipoxygenase decreasing leukotriene production
options.rationale: Wrong: Zileuton inhibits 5-lipoxygenase; cromolyn's mechanism is mast cell stabilization, not leukotriene synthesis inhibition.

options.text: Blockade of M3 receptors on smooth muscle to cause bronchodilation
options.rationale: Wrong: Anticholinergics block M3 receptors; cromolyn works by preventing mast cell degranulation, not muscarinic blockade.

options.text: Competitive inhibition of IgE binding to FcεRI on mast cells
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab binds circulating IgE to prevent FcεRI binding; cromolyn stabilizes mast cells and does not competitively inhibit IgE binding.

question: A patient with chronic asthma is switched from oral prednisone to high-dose inhaled corticosteroid. Based on the lecture, which systemic adverse effect is most likely to be reduced by this change?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Reduced risk of osteoporosis and systemic corticosteroid effects
options.rationale: Correct: Inhaled corticosteroids at lower systemic exposure reduce risks like osteopenia/osteoporosis compared with systemic corticosteroids as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Elimination of oropharyngeal candidiasis risk entirely
options.rationale: Wrong: Inhaled steroids still carry a risk of oropharyngeal candidiasis due to local deposition; switching from oral to inhaled reduces systemic effects but not local thrush risk.

options.text: Immediate cessation of adrenal suppression within hours
options.rationale: Wrong: Adrenal suppression from systemic steroids may persist and tapering is required; inhaled steroids reduce systemic exposure but do not guarantee immediate recovery of adrenal function.

options.text: Increased incidence of hepatotoxicity compared with oral therapy
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is not a typical adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids; systemic steroids are more associated with systemic metabolic effects.

options.text: Higher likelihood of neuropsychiatric adverse events than oral prednisone
options.rationale: Wrong: Systemic corticosteroids are more likely to cause neuropsychiatric effects; inhaled steroids reduce systemic exposure and thus lower such risks.

question: A patient with severe asthma has persistent symptoms despite maximal inhaled therapy and elevated IgE. The team orders omalizumab. Which monitoring concern from the lecture should be emphasized after administration?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Observe for anaphylaxis after subcutaneous injections
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture highlights rare but serious anaphylaxis with omalizumab, so post-injection observation is recommended.

options.text: Monitor liver enzymes for zileuton like hepatotoxicity
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity monitoring is relevant for zileuton, not omalizumab; the primary omalizumab concern is anaphylaxis.

options.text: Check serum theophylline levels due to interaction risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab does not interact with theophylline metabolism; theophylline level monitoring is unrelated to anti-IgE therapy.

options.text: Assess intraocular pressure for nebulized anticholinergic effects
options.rationale: Wrong: Intraocular pressure concerns relate to nebulized anticholinergics causing mydriasis; this is not the primary monitoring issue for omalizumab.

options.text: Perform depression screening due to montelukast risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Neuropsychiatric screening is relevant for montelukast; omalizumab monitoring focuses on immediate hypersensitivity reactions.

question: A patient with asthma is prescribed a combination inhaler containing budesonide and formoterol. Based on lecture content, what is the primary therapeutic advantage of this combination?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the current evidence-based GDMT for asthma/COPD (Competencies III.4; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Simultaneous bronchodilation and anti-inflammatory control improving outcomes
options.rationale: Correct: ICS-LABA combinations like budesonide-formoterol provide bronchodilation plus anti-inflammatory therapy, addressing both symptoms and underlying inflammation as the lecture recommends.

options.text: Reduced systemic absorption compared with inhaled corticosteroid alone
options.rationale: Wrong: Combination therapy does not inherently reduce systemic absorption of the steroid; the main advantage is addressing both bronchospasm and inflammation.

options.text: Direct inhibition of leukotriene synthesis and immediate relief
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene synthesis inhibition is the mechanism of zileuton; budesonide-formoterol provides steroidal anti-inflammatory effects and β2-mediated bronchodilation, not leukotriene inhibition.

options.text: Permanent cure of airway remodeling with long term use
options.rationale: Wrong: While ICS can reduce remodeling, the lecture does not claim combination inhalers permanently cure airway remodeling; they improve control and reduce exacerbations.

options.text: Elimination of need for rescue short acting bronchodilators entirely
options.rationale: Wrong: Combination inhalers improve control but do not universally eliminate the need for rescue SABAs; rescue therapy may still be required for acute attacks.

question: A patient with severe asthma has elevated IL-13 driven mucus hypersecretion. Which biologic mechanism from the lecture would most directly reduce mucus production?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Inhibition of IL-4 and IL-13 signaling by dupilumab reducing mucus
options.rationale: Correct: IL-13 promotes mucus hypersecretion; dupilumab inhibits IL-4/IL-13 signaling and can reduce mucus production as noted in the lecture.

options.text: Binding circulating IgE with omalizumab to block mucus secretion
options.rationale: Wrong: Omalizumab reduces allergic activation via IgE but does not directly inhibit IL-13 driven mucus hypersecretion; IL-4/IL-13 blockade is more direct.

options.text: Antagonism of CysLT1 receptors to directly stop mucus synthesis
options.rationale: Wrong: Leukotriene receptor antagonists reduce bronchoconstriction and edema but do not directly block IL-13 mediated mucus hypersecretion.

options.text: Stabilization of mast cells with cromolyn to eliminate mucus production
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn prevents mediator release but does not directly inhibit IL-13 signaling responsible for mucus hypersecretion.

options.text: PDE inhibition by theophylline to reduce mucus via cAMP increase
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibitors increase cAMP and have some anti-inflammatory effects but are not the targeted IL-13 pathway inhibitors described for mucus hypersecretion.

question: A patient with COPD is intolerant of nicotine replacement and bupropion. The clinician considers varenicline. Based on the lecture, what dual pharmacologic actions explain its efficacy?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Partial agonism at α4β2 receptors and competitive nicotine blockade
options.rationale: Correct: Varenicline is a partial agonist at α4β2 nicotinic receptors providing some dopamine release and competitively blocking nicotine binding, reducing reward and cravings as the lecture explains.

options.text: Full agonism at α4β2 receptors producing maximal dopamine release
options.rationale: Wrong: Varenicline is a partial, not full, agonist; full agonism would produce stronger reward and not reduce nicotine's reinforcing effects.

options.text: Inhibition of norepinephrine reuptake increasing withdrawal symptoms
options.rationale: Wrong: Bupropion inhibits NE and dopamine reuptake; varenicline acts at nicotinic receptors rather than monoamine reuptake.

options.text: Antagonism of α4β2 receptors preventing any receptor activation
options.rationale: Wrong: Varenicline is a partial agonist, not a pure antagonist; pure antagonism would block receptor activity but not provide partial agonist mitigation of withdrawal.

options.text: Activation of muscarinic receptors reducing nicotine craving centrally
options.rationale: Wrong: Muscarinic receptor activation is unrelated to varenicline's mechanism; varenicline targets nicotinic α4β2 receptors specifically.

question: A patient with asthma is taking high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and develops delayed growth concerns in a child. Based on the lecture, which counseling point is most consistent with the slides?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids can delay growth and require lowest effective dose
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes delayed growth in children as an adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids and recommends using the lowest effective dose.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids cause immediate adrenal crisis in children
options.rationale: Wrong: Immediate adrenal crisis is not the typical effect of inhaled steroids at therapeutic doses; growth delay is the specific pediatric concern highlighted in the lecture.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids increase leukotriene production worsening asthma
options.rationale: Wrong: Corticosteroids reduce many proinflammatory mediators; they do not increase leukotriene production as a typical adverse effect.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids commonly cause hepatotoxicity in pediatric patients
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is not a common adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids; the lecture emphasizes growth delay and bone effects.

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroids produce tremor via peripheral β2 receptor stimulation
options.rationale: Wrong: Tremor is associated with β2 agonists; inhaled corticosteroids do not stimulate β2 receptors and are not the cause of tremor.

question: A patient with asthma is prescribed zileuton. Which laboratory monitoring and adverse effect from the lecture should the clinician prioritize?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Monitor liver enzymes due to risk of hepatotoxicity with zileuton
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists hepatotoxicity as a key adverse effect of zileuton, necessitating liver enzyme monitoring.

options.text: Monitor serum theophylline levels for CYP3A induction interactions
options.rationale: Wrong: Theophylline monitoring is relevant for CYP3A interactions with inhibitors like azoles; zileuton hepatotoxicity monitoring is the priority for zileuton therapy.

options.text: Check intraocular pressure for nebulized anticholinergic side effects
options.rationale: Wrong: Intraocular pressure monitoring is relevant for nebulized anticholinergics; zileuton requires hepatic monitoring instead.

options.text: Screen for depression due to montelukast associated suicide risk
options.rationale: Wrong: Neuropsychiatric screening is pertinent to montelukast; zileuton’s main concern per the lecture is hepatotoxicity.

options.text: Obtain ECG monitoring for immediate arrhythmia risk from zileuton
options.rationale: Wrong: Arrhythmias are associated with methylxanthine toxicity; zileuton’s primary adverse effect is hepatotoxicity rather than acute cardiac arrhythmia.

question: A patient with asthma uses a LABA with a lipophilic side chain that prolongs duration. Which pharmacologic property described in the lecture explains this prolonged action?
cited_learning_objective: Explain the molecular mechanisms of action of each drug class for treating asthma/COPD (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Lipophilic side chain anchors drug in the airway membrane prolonging effect
options.rationale: Correct: LABAs like salmeterol have engineered lipophilic side chains that prolong duration by anchoring in the airway membrane as described in the lecture.

options.text: Rapid hepatic metabolism producing a long lasting active metabolite
options.rationale: Wrong: Rapid hepatic metabolism would shorten duration; the lecture attributes prolonged LABA action to lipophilic membrane anchoring, not hepatic metabolites.

options.text: Irreversible β2 receptor antagonism causing prolonged bronchodilation
options.rationale: Wrong: LABAs are agonists, not irreversible antagonists; prolonged effect is due to lipophilicity and membrane retention rather than receptor antagonism.

options.text: Enhanced renal clearance leading to accumulation and longer action
options.rationale: Wrong: Enhanced renal clearance would reduce accumulation and shorten action; this does not explain LABA prolonged duration.

options.text: Inhibition of phosphodiesterase III producing sustained cAMP elevation
options.rationale: Wrong: PDE inhibition (theophylline) increases cAMP but is not the mechanism for LABA prolonged membrane-anchored duration described in the lecture.

question: A patient with asthma is prescribed montelukast for allergic rhinitis and asthma control. Which formulation advantage from the lecture supports this choice in children?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Oral tablet formulation easier for children improving adherence
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture notes montelukast's tablet formulation is easier for children and increases likelihood of delivery and adherence.

options.text: Inhaled delivery minimizing systemic exposure in pediatric patients
options.rationale: Wrong: Montelukast is oral; inhaled delivery minimizes systemic exposure for steroids but is not the formulation advantage cited for montelukast in children.

options.text: Subcutaneous injection providing monthly dosing convenience
options.rationale: Wrong: Subcutaneous biologics like omalizumab are not the oral tablet advantage described for montelukast in pediatric use.

options.text: Nebulized solution allowing four times daily dosing flexibility
options.rationale: Wrong: Cromolyn nebulization requires frequent dosing; montelukast's advantage is oral tablet ease, not nebulized administration.

options.text: Transdermal patch delivering steady leukotriene blockade
options.rationale: Wrong: Transdermal patches are not the montelukast formulation discussed; the lecture highlights oral tablets as advantageous for children.

question: A patient with asthma is using high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and reports bone pain. Based on the lecture, which long-term adverse effect is most consistent with chronic corticosteroid exposure?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the major adverse effects, drug interactions, and contraindications of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Osteopenia and osteoporosis from chronic corticosteroid exposure
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture lists osteopenia and osteoporosis as adverse effects of chronic corticosteroid therapy.

options.text: Acute angle closure glaucoma from inhaled steroid deposition
options.rationale: Wrong: Angle closure glaucoma is associated with nebulized anticholinergics causing mydriasis; corticosteroids are linked to bone loss rather than acute glaucoma in the lecture.

options.text: Hepatotoxicity requiring routine liver enzyme monitoring
options.rationale: Wrong: Hepatotoxicity is a concern with zileuton; corticosteroids are not primarily hepatotoxic per the lecture.

options.text: Seizures and toxic encephalopathy from inhaled steroid overdose
options.rationale: Wrong: Seizures are associated with methylxanthine toxicity; inhaled corticosteroids do not typically cause seizures or toxic encephalopathy.

options.text: Immediate tachycardia and arrhythmia from inhaled steroid use
options.rationale: Wrong: Tachycardia and arrhythmias are adverse effects of adrenergic agonists and methylxanthines, not inhaled corticosteroids which cause bone and growth effects.

question: A patient with asthma has type I hypersensitivity mediated by IgE crosslinking on mast cells. Which immediate mediators released after degranulation are emphasized in the lecture as causing bronchoconstriction?
cited_learning_objective: Describe the pharmacological effects of each drug class (Competencies II.1; OMED620.2,12)

options.text: Histamine and leukotrienes released from mast cell degranulation
options.rationale: Correct: The lecture describes IgE-mediated mast cell degranulation releasing histamine and leukotrienes which contribute to bronchoconstriction.

options.text: Dopamine and serotonin released causing bronchial dilation
options.rationale: Wrong: Dopamine and serotonin are not the primary mediators of IgE-mediated bronchoconstriction described in the lecture; histamine and leukotrienes are.

options.text: Insulin and glucagon release leading to airway smooth muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Wrong: Insulin and glucagon are metabolic hormones unrelated to mast cell mediated bronchoconstriction.

options.text: Acetylcholine release from mast cells causing bronchospasm
options.rationale: Wrong: Acetylcholine is released from parasympathetic nerves acting on M3 receptors; mast cell degranulation primarily releases histamine and leukotrienes.

options.text: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin causing airway edema and constriction
options.rationale: Wrong: Nitric oxide and prostacyclin are vasodilatory mediators and not the main bronchoconstrictive mediators released by mast cell IgE crosslinking per the lecture.
